summary: Students will be introduced to the Everglades and learn that it is a place of watery wonder that they can explore using their senses
prekDomains: VIII. Creative Expression Through the Arts

summary: Students will use science processing skills such as classifying, communicating, measuring, and observing to describe living and non-living natural “treasures” found in the Everglades
Students will learn that plants, such as grasses, are an important part of the Everglades by crafting their own native grass project
Students will craft their own set of binoculars to identify animals in the Everglades through a search activity
prekDomains: VIII. Creative Expression through the Arts

summary: Students will explore and begin to identify animals in the Everglades and how they move during a creative expression of movement activity
prekDomains: VIII. Creative Expression through the Arts

summary: Students will be introduced to the Everglades, learning about this special place for plants and animals that is unlike anywhere else on Earth
Students will review the similarities and differences between some of the animals that live in the Everglades
Students will engage in an interactive presentation to review some of the animals that live in the Everglades
Students will learn that animals communicate through their senses
Students will be introduced to the plants and wildlife that live in different habitats of the Everglades
Students will discuss and identify the different ways humans and animals use water
Students will read a book on the importance of American alligators and act out a short play which demonstrates the dangers of feeding wild animals
Students will act out an ecodrama in an alligator hole during the dry season
Students will be learning about changing water levels in the Everglades and how it affects the amount of food available for wading birds, such as the Wood Stork

Students will learn that animals can be classified into six major animal groups and become familiar with Everglades animals in these groups. Students will also learn about the five different habitats of the Everglades, as well as the different animals that live in each one.
Students will identify some of the flowering and nonflowering plants of the Everglades using a dichotomous key and learn about the five different habitats of the Everglades where these plants live.
Students will use a relay race activity to reinforce knowledge learned in Lesson 1 - Classifying Everglades Animals and Their Habitats and Lesson 2 - Classifying Everglades Plants and Their Habitats.
Students will learn about specific Everglades producers, consumers, and food chains by role-playing.
Students will read a book titled Everglades by Jean Craighead George. They will research a threatened or endangered animal species and create a poster of their findings.
Students will play a game that demonstrates how animal populations can be negatively impacted by humans.
Students will become Florida panthers, white-tailed deer, and motor vehicles in an active, tag-like game to simulate the disappearance of Everglades habitat and its effect on native wildlife.

Students will examine the effects of exotic and invasive species in an ecosystem using riddles and research. Students will be able to explain how exotic and invasive species can harm native species or habitats in the Everglades.

Students will examine the effect of exotic species on an ecosystem by role-playing both a healthy food chain, and a food chain that has been impacted by Mayan cichlids. In the process of role-playing, students will compare and contrast the adaptations of a native species and an exotic species.
Students will be able to identify locations and waterways in the Kissimmee-Lake Okeechobee-Everglades (K-O-E) watershed on a map after watching a video and reading a story.

Students will demonstrate how rainfall is a driving force in the KOE Watershed and analyze how rainfall data reveals patterns that are a defining characteristic of the Everglades climate: our wet and dry seasons.

Through building a wetland model, students will learn how wetlands in the Everglades function and why it is important to protect them. Students will then associate objects as metaphors for the natural functions of wetlands.
Students will explore the important relationships of aquifers to the Everglades and residents of southern Florida and build an aquifer model.
Students will use the aquifer model from the previous lesson to discuss pollution, how it affects the Everglades, and the different ways we use water.

Students will participate in a lab experiment where they identify the different water users in the Everglades and how much water is consumed by each user group. Students will recognize ways to conserve water and discuss why water conservation is important to the Everglades.

Students will be presented with different "water dilemmas" affecting the Everglades. Teams will analyze the different scenarios, select which action they would take related to the dilemmas, and justify their reasonings.

In small groups, students build a landscape model to illustrate the uniqueness of the Kissimmee-Lake Okeechobee-Everglades (K-O-E) watershed, and then modify the model to demonstrate how alterations have affected the K-O-E watershed.

In order to compare weather, climate, and other environmental factors of the K-O-E watershed to other places on or near the 28th parallel, students will trace the latitude of the Everglades and different locations around the world.
Students will learn about Everglades ecosystems by “traveling” through the plant communities of the Everglades watershed.

Students learn about the unique adaptations mangroves have that allow them to live in coastal communities. Students construct models to demonstrate how mangroves help protect shorelines and contribute to the growth of the peninsula.
Students become "bioengineers" by engineering an animal that is adapted to a specific Everglades ecosystem, creating the "perfect beast".
Students will explain the concepts of "ecotone" and "edge effect", and use a diagram to describe how this relates to biological diversity.
Students explore the costs and environmental impacts of land development and restoration.

Using the Restudy, students will evaluate the conditions of our watershed that prompted the development of the Comprehensive Everglades Restoration Plan (CERP) and evaluate whether or not they think CERP addresses these issues.
Students will analyze information about various current and ongoing Comprehensive Everglades Restoration Plan (CERP) projects and report on the progress that is being made.
Students will explore how the common usage of a potentially renewable resources can lead to its exploitation.
Students will look at a typical water conservation plan and analyze it from the viewpoint of various stakeholders.
Students will learn about Everglades water quality management and will analyze sample data from a Stormwater Treatment Area (STA).
